analysis.one_liner: Directs federal safety agencies to study workplace violence and issue voluntary, nonbinding guidance on preventing it.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to committee in April 2025 and has received no action since, with a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health study how to reduce violence at work — including threats and attacks with weapons or common objects — and report recommendations to the Labor Department within 15 months. Within 4 years, OSHA would then issue guidance tailored to each type of workplace, from grocery stores and hospitals to schools and bars, covering things like weapon detectors, shatter-resistant glass, security staffing, and worker de-escalation training. The guidance would be nonmandatory: no employer would be required to follow it.
analysis.who_benefits: If it becomes law, the guidance would mainly serve workers in high-contact jobs — grocery clerks, retail workers, nurses, teachers, restaurant staff — who face the highest risk of being threatened or attacked by customers, patients, or visitors. Because the guidance is voluntary, its practical benefit depends entirely on employers choosing to adopt the recommendations.

how_it_helps.text: Directs NIOSH to study how to reduce the threat of violence at work and recommend measures to the Labor Department.

Requires OSHA, within 4 years, to issue guidance tailored to specific workplace types — grocery stores, hospitals, schools, restaurants, and others — covering engineering controls like weapon detectors, shatter-resistant glass, and cameras, plus staffing, security personnel, and de-escalation training.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who voluntarily adopt the guidance would bear the cost of security equipment, staffing changes, and training. As written, no one is required to pay anything.
analysis.who_pays_short: No one, unless employers adopt it

drawbacks.text: The guidance is explicitly nonmandatory, so no employer is required to make any of the recommended changes; the bill would not by itself force a single store or hospital to add a barrier, a guard, or a training.
The timeline is slow: the study takes up to 15 months and OSHA would not have to issue the guidance until 4 years after enactment [S2], meaning no practical effect for years.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is low-cost and could genuinely improve worker safety, but it is also deliberately weak: it produces only recommendations, not rules, and on a four-year timeline, so any employer that wants to ignore the guidance can. An honest supporter would acknowledge that this is a first step designed to avoid triggering enforcement fights, not a fix for workplace violence itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee in April 2025 and nothing has happened to it since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 3, 2025 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.
No further action has been taken: no hearing, no markup, no vote, and no committee report appear in the action history.
It has just one cosponsor, a Democrat.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers opposed to any new workplace-safety expectations are better off for now, since a committee reference with no movement costs them nothing.

sides.party_line_note: With one sponsor and one cosponsor, both Democrats, there is no visible bipartisan support or organized opposition yet.

industries.industry: Retail, grocery, restaurant, and service employers
industries.note: These are the workplaces most exposed to customer violence and would be the focus of the guidance; nothing would be required of them, but adopting recommendations could add costs for security equipment, staffing, and training. Workers in these industries would benefit if the guidance leads to real protections.

Hospitals are singled out as a high-risk workplace type; they already face violence from patients and visitors and would face expectations about staffing and training, though the guidance would carry no legal force.

analysis.trajectory: With a single cosponsor, no hearing or markup scheduled, and referral to a committee controlled by the opposing party, the bill is very likely to die quietly at the end of the Congress without a vote.
